title: United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications, Inc.
shortTitle: United States Naval Institute v. Charter Communications
summary: Compensation for early paperback sales rested on lost hardcover profits, rather than an automatic transfer of the breaching publisher’s gains.
notes:
Court: Second Circuit (1991).

Study caution: $35,380.50 and $7,760.12 had different legal bases and different outcomes. The case does not announce that every profitable breach is socially efficient or legally privileged.

sections.Parties: United States Naval Institute held the hardcover publishing interest in The Hunt for Red October. Charter, the paperback licensee, published through Berkley.
sections.Material Facts: The paperback agreement restricted the beginning of sales until October. Books reached retail sale in mid-September. Shipment practices and retail sale were distinct: distributing stock to retailers before the date was not necessarily itself a breach. Early sales competed with the Institute’s hardcover sales.
sections.Procedural History: An initial ruling rejecting liability was reversed on an earlier appeal. After remand, the district court awarded $35,380.50 for lost hardcover profits and an additional $7,760.12 linked to copyright profits. On the appeal reproduced here, the Second Circuit upheld the compensatory award and reversed the additional profits award.
sections.Issue: What loss did the premature sales cause the promisee, and did the licensee’s breach also justify recovery of profits as copyright infringement?
sections.Holding: The reasonable estimate of the Institute’s lost hardcover profits was sustained. Charter’s sale within its license, although contractually premature, did not make it an infringer entitled to disgorge profits under the asserted copyright measure.
sections.Reasoning: The relevant benchmark is the loss attributable to breach, not all paperback profits. The factfinder could infer lost September hardcover sales from the available sales history without mathematical precision. Uncertainty caused by the wrongdoer does not entitle it to an artificially low estimate, but an award still must be compensatory. The opinion separates a licensee’s contractual violation from use outside the copyright license. It also explains why greater gains to the party in breach do not automatically supply the promisee’s contract damages.
